ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Consultation — Clara Barton — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week sertraline tolerability and safety check, with psychiatry consultation

text.paragraph: Recurrent, moderately severe depressive episode in a 52-year-old nurse and relief-agency director four months after an eighteen-month wartime deployment. Please confirm the diagnosis, exclude bipolar disorder and PTSD, and advise on treatment, duration, and return to work. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within two weeks; no current suicidal ideation. [S]

list.item: Do you confirm recurrent major depressive disorder, and are there features of bipolar disorder, PTSD, or a psychotic depression?
Is combined sertraline and cognitive behavioral therapy the right treatment, and what dose and titration do you advise?
Do you agree with the suicide-risk assessment and the safety plan?
How long should treatment continue after remission, given that this is a recurrent episode?
What do you advise about her return to work and any future deployment?

text.paragraph: Ms. Barton is seen at the request of Dr. Whitcombe, two weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg. She describes about four months of low mood, loss of interest, fatigue, early waking, poor concentration, low appetite, and a sense of being useless since her return from a long war-zone deployment, with an earlier, milder episode in her forties after another deployment. She has never had a period of elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, or risky behavior. She saw distressing scenes in the field but has no intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance, or hypervigilance that trouble her. She has had no hallucinations or delusions. She has never attempted suicide or harmed herself and has no suicidal thoughts now. She drinks one or two glasses of wine a week and uses no drugs. She tolerated the first week of sertraline with mild nausea that has settled. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Clarissa Harlowe Barton was born on December 25, 1821, in North Oxford, Massachusetts, the youngest of five children. [D]
Her diary records a brief period of depression in the spring of 1852, while she was teaching in New Jersey; her biographer judged that the mood did not last long. [D]

From 1861 she supplied and tended wounded soldiers at battlefields and field hospitals through the Civil War; after working for several days following the Battle of Antietam in September 1862 she was weakened by typhoid fever. [D]
In her account of the eve of the Battle of Antietam she wrote that she was faint but could not eat, weary but could not sleep, and depressed but could not weep. [D]
From March 1865 to 1869 she ran an office that answered 63,182 letters and identified 22,000 missing soldiers. [D]

In December 1868 she lost her voice while giving a lecture, from fatigue and mental prostration; in her own later account, nervous prostration had declared itself and she lay helpless all winter in Washington. [D]
In September 1869, on her doctor's advice, she travelled to Europe to regain her health. [D]
During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and 1871 she organized civilian relief in Strasbourg, Paris, and other French cities. [D]

In 1872 and 1873 she suffered nervous exhaustion and temporarily lost her eyesight; in a letter she wrote that she broke down with a cough in England in October 1872 and was confined to bed for eight months. [D]

After her return in October 1873 she broke down again with what she called prostration of the nervous system, deepened by her only sister's death in May 1874; she wrote that for almost a year she averaged less than two hours of sleep a day and could not write her name for over four months. [D]
A 1995 review by Spiegel describes her long-term nervous prostration and argues that the therapy she received changed her behavioral approach to illness and to life. [R]
Her biographer Elizabeth Brown Pryor, as quoted in a 2012 newspaper article, describes a long struggle with depression that was lifted by a need for her services. [R]
Her mother died on July 18, 1851, and her father on March 21, 1862. [D]

text.paragraph: 3 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

tr.td: Sertraline 50 mg oral tablet, one tablet by mouth each morning
One tablet by mouth each morning

Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate (moderately severe symptoms at intake), after a prolonged humanitarian deployment; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented periods of depression and nervous prostration

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. Her periods of depression and nervous prostration are documented in her own words (D); calling them major depression is a retrospective interpretation (R), and no diagnosis was made in her lifetime.
Occupational burnout after eighteen months leading field medical relief in a war zone
S — Synthetic contributing factor echoing her documented exhaustion after wartime relief work; burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a mental disorder.

list.item: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate (F33.1). Confirmed: a recurrent major depressive episode of moderate to moderately severe intensity, without psychotic features. No history of mania or hypomania, so bipolar disorder is unlikely. PTSD criteria are not met, with a negative screen and no re-experiencing or avoidance. Anxiety symptoms are part of the depressive episode. Acute suicide risk is low: no ideation, intent, plan, or past suicidal behavior, no firearms, and strong protective factors; the safety plan is appropriate. [S]

Occupational burnout (Z73.0). A strong contributor, from years of high-intensity relief work without leave. It does not replace the depression diagnosis, and rest alone will not treat the depression. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: The intake history, PHQ-9 of 18 and today's 16, GAD-7, PC-PTSD-5, AUDIT-C, the laboratory results, and the collaborative safety plan. [S]

list.item: Continue sertraline 50 mg; if the PHQ-9 has fallen by less than 50 percent at about six weeks, increase to 100 mg, then review four to six weeks later. [S]
Weekly cognitive behavioral therapy for about 16 sessions, with behavioral activation and insomnia components; combined treatment is appropriate for a recurrent episode. [S]
PHQ-9 at least monthly until remission, and suicide-risk review with the safety plan at every visit. [S]
Continue sertraline for at least twelve months after remission because the episode is recurrent, then review tapering or maintenance. [S]

Phased return to work after the medical leave, starting at no more than 25 hours a week and building to a limit of about 45 hours, with no field deployment for at least six months and a relief workers' peer support group. [S]
Explain that prolonged rest or withdrawal from activity is not a treatment for depression; structured activity, sleep regularity, and social contact are. [S]
Return to psychiatry if there is no response twelve weeks after reaching 100 mg, if suicidal thoughts emerge, or if mood elevation appears. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Whitcombe the same day; Ms. Barton agrees with the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Primary care manages treatment with the clinic psychologist. Psychiatry is available for a further consultation on the criteria above. [S]
